answer.label: Not Cicero — Taylor Caldwell, in a 1965 novel
answer.authorDates: 1900–1985 · British-born American novelist of historical fiction
answer.sourceLine: The passage was written by Taylor Caldwell for her 1965 novel A Pillar of Iron, where it appears on page 483 as narration summarising the fictional Cicero’s own position, which a fictional Antonius is said to agree with — not words Cicero speaks aloud. Louisiana Congressman Otto E. Passman recast it as a direct Cicero quotation in a House Appropriations subcommittee hearing on 4 May 1966, swapping “the arrogance of the generals” for “the arrogance of officialdom,” and it has circulated as Cicero ever since. It is in none of Cicero’s speeches, letters or treatises.

source.heading: Where the words actually come from

docMeta.dd: Taylor Caldwell — as narration, not as dialogue
1965 · Doubleday, Garden City, N.Y. · passage on p. 483
4 May 1966 · Rep. Otto E. Passman, House Appropriations subcommittee hearing

source.excerpt: Mr. PASSMAN. The committee will come to order. You know occasionally in our busy and bored lives we run into interesting, well written books of history. The path that we are traveling is a complete duplication of great nations that preceded us in greatness and finally fell by their foolishness. I would like to quote one or two items for the record. I am quoting them verbatim. One— The budget should be balanced, the treasury should be refilled, public debt should be reduced, the arrogance of officialdom should be tempered and controlled, assistance to foreign lands should be curtailed lest Rome become bankrupt, the mob should be forced to work and not depend on government for subsistence, and prudence and frugality should be put into practice. Cicero, 58 B.C.
trail: 1965 — Taylor Caldwell publishes A Pillar of Iron (Doubleday, Garden City, N.Y.). On page 483, narration summarises the fictional Cicero’s own position — a balanced budget, a refilled Treasury, reduced public debt, curtailed assistance to foreign lands — which a fictional Gaius Antonius Hybrida heartily agrees with. Cicero never speaks the words. Wikiquote records the page, and p. 371 of the 1966 Collins edition ↗

4 May 1966 — Rep. Otto E. Passman of Louisiana reads it into a House Appropriations subcommittee hearing as a verbatim quotation from Cicero, dated 58 B.C., with “the arrogance of the generals” changed to “officialdom.” A Chicago Tribune column carries it that 16 November. Quote Investigator documents both ↗

25 April 1968 — Passman reads the passage into the Congressional Record as Cicero’s warning about share-the-wealth programs, and repeats it to Secretary of State Dean Rusk at a hearing that May. Snopes prints the Congressional Record text ↗

1971, then 1989 — Prof. John H. Collins offers $50 to the Chicago Tribune letter-writer’s favourite charity if anyone can cite chapter and verse for it anywhere in Cicero, and names page 483 as its real home; the Congressional Research Service later rules in Respectfully Quoted that no evidence confirms Cicero said the words and it is almost certainly spurious. Both are quoted at Quote Investigator ↗
source.excerptNote: This is the moment the line became a quotation: a US House subcommittee hearing, 4 May 1966, printed by the Government Printing Office. Passman says he is quoting verbatim from a book of history — he is in fact quoting a novel published the year before, and he has changed it. Caldwell’s sentence is indirect narration summarising the fictional Cicero’s own position, which Antonius is said to agree with, and it reads “the arrogance of the generals,” not of officialdom.

source.rightsNote: The wording originates in Taylor Caldwell’s A Pillar of Iron, published by Doubleday in 1965 — far too recent to be public domain in the United States, so the underlying passage is in copyright to her estate and publisher. Nothing here is a public-domain ancient text: Cicero’s own Latin has been free for two millennia, but this sentence is not Cicero’s. The circulating rewrite — “officialdom” for “the generals,” the added “public assistance” sentence — has no identifiable author, so its status is unsettled; treat the whole passage as protected rather than free. The 1966 hearing transcript excerpted above is a US Government Printing Office document and is in the public domain.

author.name: Taylor Caldwell
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: 1900–1985 · British-born American novelist of historical fiction
author.bio: Janet Miriam Taylor Caldwell was born in Manchester, England in 1900 and died in Greenwich, Connecticut in 1985. She built a long career on sweeping historical and religious novels — Dear and Glorious Physician on Saint Luke, The Earth Is the Lord’s on Genghis Khan, and the best-selling Captains and the Kings — and A Pillar of Iron (1965) was her novel about Cicero. Her foreword advertised years of research and hundreds of Cicero letters translated in the Vatican Library, which is a large part of why readers took her invented lines for documented history.

misattribution.heading: What’s wrong with the version you saw
misattribution.intro: Almost every element of the popular version is manufactured — the speaker, the date, and several of the words themselves.

items.why: The passage is in none of Cicero’s speeches, letters or treatises. Quote Investigator ↗ traces it to page 483 of Taylor Caldwell’s 1965 novel A Pillar of Iron, and Wikiquote ↗ lists it under Misattributed for the same reason.

Both dates were attached after the fact. Rep. Otto E. Passman labelled it “58 B.C.” in his 1966 hearing testimony; the “55 B.C.” label spread later, and by 1992 a San Francisco Chronicle column was reporting a “55 B.C.” version copied off a poster in a São Paulo notary’s office — both documented at Quote Investigator ↗.

Caldwell’s sentence has the arrogance of the generals, and Snopes ↗ notes that the circulating version now refers to generic officialdom rather than military figures. The swap is already there in Passman’s 1966 hearing text, printed at Quote Investigator ↗.

items.who: “People must again learn to work, instead of living on public assistance”
items.why: Caldwell wrote that the mobs should be forced to work and not depend on government for subsistence. The “public assistance” phrasing is a later rewrite; Quote Investigator ↗ records it in a 1992 newspaper version of the saying.

misattribution.truthLine: Cicero did argue something adjacent, in his own words: in the Pro Sestio he described Gaius Gracchus’s grain law as popular because it supplied food without labour, and opposed by the good men because it would draw people from industry to idleness and drain the treasury — Pro Sestio, chapter 48 at Perseus ↗. That is a real Roman argument about a real Roman law, and it is not the quotation on the poster.

context.heading: How a novelist’s sentence became a Roman senator’s warning
lead: Caldwell’s novel is not a forgery — it is a novel, and it never claims Cicero said this. The sentence on page 483 is narration: a summary of the fictional Cicero’s own position, which a fictional Gaius Antonius Hybrida heartily agreed with, before the imagined conversation turns to how any of it would be paid for. What made the line so portable was the foreword, in which Caldwell described translating hundreds of Cicero’s letters herself and told readers that wherever the book says “Cicero wrote,” the letters are authentic. Readers generalised that promise to the whole book.

The passage entered public life in 1966, when Rep. Otto E. Passman of Louisiana — who spent three decades in Congress fighting foreign-aid spending — read it into a House Appropriations subcommittee hearing as a verbatim quotation, dated it “58 B.C.,” and changed “the arrogance of the generals” to “the arrogance of officialdom.” A Chicago Tribune column carried it that November, Passman repeated it to Secretary of State Dean Rusk in 1968, and from there it moved through letters pages, columns and eventually cable news, shedding and gaining clauses each time. The closing sentence in today’s most common version — “People must again learn to work, instead of living on public assistance” — is not in the novel at all.
detailsBody: In March 1971 a Chicago Tribune reader quoted the passage as Cicero’s warning to a bankrupting Rome. The following month the paper printed a reply from John H. Collins, Professor of History at Northern Illinois University, who offered to contribute $50 to that reader’s favourite charity if he or anyone else could cite chapter and verse for it anywhere in Cicero’s known writings, identified page 483 of A Pillar of Iron as its actual home, and noted that a novelist may invent conversations but should not present them as authentic history. Quote Investigator credits researcher Bonnie Taylor-Blake with locating both the letter and the passage in the novel.

In 1989 the Congressional Research Service, asked about it often enough to publish a ruling, entered the quotation in Respectfully Quoted: A Dictionary of Quotations with the verdict that no evidence had been found to confirm Cicero said the words and that the saying is almost certainly spurious. The attribution has nevertheless outlived every debunking of it: a CNN host offered a trimmed version as something Cicero “is believed to have said” in 2011.
context.pull: No evidence has been found to confirm that Cicero said these words, and it is almost certainly spurious.

sourcesVerified.claim: There is no substantive evidence Cicero spoke or wrote these words; the quotation derives from Taylor Caldwell's 1965 novel A Pillar of Iron, p. 483, where it is the narrated inner view of the fictional Cicero and is not spoken aloud; Rep. Otto E. Passman used it as a direct Cicero quote in a May 1966 congressional subcommittee hearing (4 May 1966, p. 673), changing 'arrogance of the generals' to 'arrogance of officialdom' and dating it 58 B.C.; Chicago Tribune 16 Nov 1966; Passman repeated it to Dean Rusk 22 May 1968; John H. Collins's 20 April 1971 Chicago Tribune letter offered $50 and named p. 483; the 1989 Congressional Research Service Respectfully Quoted concluded 'No evidence has been found to confirm that Cicero said these words, and it is almost certainly spurious'; a 1992 Herb Caen column carried a '55 B.C.' version using the phrase 'public assistance'; a 2011 CNN broadcast used a trimmed version.

Snopes rates the claim False, states the words were never uttered by Cicero and were not written until 1965 by Taylor Caldwell, prints the fuller novel passage identifying the interlocutor as Gaius Antonius Hybrida and showing 'the arrogance of the generals', and quotes Rep. Otto Passman reading the line into the Congressional Record on April 25, 1968.

Wikiquote's Cicero article lists the passage under the heading 'Misattributed', stating the quotes come from a novel about Cicero by Taylor Caldwell and are not found in any of Cicero's actual writings, and cites A Pillar of Iron (1965), p. 483 of the 1965 Doubleday (Garden City, NY) edition and p. 371, chapter 51 of the 1966 Collins (London) edition.

The University of Texas at Austin Cicero site's myths page states 'The passage is from Taylor Caldwell, A Pillar of Iron (1965)', notes the passage is frequently cited in conservative writings beginning with a 1968 Congressional Record speech, and observes that budgets and foreign assistance would have needed explaining to Cicero.

Cicero, Pro Sestio chapter 48 (section 103) genuinely discusses Gaius Gracchus proposing a corn law pleasing to the common people because food was supplied in abundance without trouble, opposed by the good because it would lead the people from industry to idleness and drain the treasury.
The Internet Archive item is a scan of A Pillar of Iron by Caldwell, Taylor, 1900-1985, published Garden City, N.Y.: Doubleday, 1965 — the edition cited for the passage.

Taylor Caldwell was born Janet Miriam Caldwell on 7 September 1900 in Manchester, England, died 30 August 1985 in Greenwich, Connecticut, was a British-born American writer of historical and religious fiction whose works include Dear and Glorious Physician, The Earth is the Lord's and Captains and the Kings, and wrote A Pillar of Iron (1965) about the Roman senator and orator Cicero.
